We later relate smooth cofibrations to smooth neighborhood deformation retracts. The notion of smooth neighborhood deformation retract gives rise to an analogous result that a closed Fr\"olicher subspace $A$ of the Fr\"olicher space $X$ is a smooth neighborhood deformation retract of $X$ if and only if the inclusion $i: A\hookrightarrow X$ comes from a certain subclass of cofibrations. In the category of Frölicher spaces, the classical topological definition of a cofibration must be modified to reflect the requirements of smoothness. A direct translation of the usual homotopy extension property is often too restrictive, because smooth homotopies cannot always be glued or reparametrized in the same way as continuous ones. Smooth cofibrations are therefore defined using a weakened form of the homotopy extension property that is compatible with the smooth structures on the spaces involved.

A central technical device in this definition is the use of **flattened unit intervals**. These are smooth models of the interval equipped with reparametrizations that are constant, or sufficiently flat, near the endpoints. Flattening eliminates the loss of smoothness that may occur when homotopies are concatenated or extended piecewise. As a result, smooth homotopy extensions can be constructed by the same general geometric ideas used in topology while remaining smooth in the Frölicher sense.

This notion of smooth cofibration is closely connected with smooth neighborhood deformation retracts. If \(A\) is a closed Frölicher subspace of a Frölicher space \(X\), one may ask whether \(A\) admits a smooth neighborhood \(U\subseteq X\) that deforms smoothly onto \(A\), with the deformation fixing every point of \(A\). Under the appropriate endpoint and stationarity conditions supplied by flattened intervals, such deformation-retract data provide precisely the controlled extension behavior required of a cofibration.

More specifically, a closed Frölicher subspace \(A\subseteq X\) is a smooth neighborhood deformation retract if and only if its inclusion
\[
i\colon A\hookrightarrow X
\]
belongs to the distinguished subclass of smooth cofibrations satisfying the relevant closedness and endpoint-control conditions. This characterization is the smooth analogue of the classical relationship between cofibrations and neighborhood deformation retract pairs. It gives both a geometric interpretation of these cofibrations and a practical criterion for recognizing them.

As an application, this framework permits the construction of the **right Puppe sequence** in the category of Frölicher spaces. Starting from a suitable smooth cofibration \(i\colon A\hookrightarrow X\), one forms the corresponding smooth mapping cone and then iterates suspension and cone constructions. The flattened-interval machinery ensures that the attaching maps, quotient constructions, and connecting morphisms are compatible with smooth homotopy. One consequently obtains a sequence of the form
\[
A \longrightarrow X \longrightarrow C_i
   \longrightarrow \Sigma A \longrightarrow \Sigma X
   \longrightarrow \Sigma C_i \longrightarrow \cdots ,
\]
where \(C_i\) denotes the smooth mapping cone of \(i\) and \(\Sigma\) denotes smooth suspension. Thus, the weakened notion of cofibration supplies enough homotopical structure to reproduce an important classical construction within the smooth setting of Frölicher spaces.

A Frölicher space is a set equipped with compatible families of smooth curves and smooth real-valued functions. Although homotopy theory can be developed in this category, the ordinary unit interval is not always an appropriate parameter object: piecewise-defined homotopies and concatenations may fail to be smooth at their joining points. To avoid this problem, one uses a flattened interval. Concretely, time is reparametrized by a smooth map that is constant near \(0\) and \(1\). Homotopies parameterized in this way are stationary near their endpoints, so they can be concatenated and extended without introducing nonsmooth corners.

Accordingly, an inclusion \(i\colon A\hookrightarrow X\) is called a cofibration when it satisfies a smooth homotopy extension property with respect to flattened homotopies. Thus, given a smooth map \(f\colon X\to Y\) and a smooth homotopy
\[
h\colon A\times I\longrightarrow Y
\]
starting at \(f|_A\), with the required flattening near the ends of \(I\), there is a smooth homotopy
\[
H\colon X\times I\longrightarrow Y
\]
such that \(H|_{A\times I}=h\) and \(H(-,0)=f\). This is weaker than demanding the extension property for every homotopy formed with the ordinary smooth structure on the interval, but it is strong enough for the usual homotopy-theoretic constructions.

The geometric counterpart of this condition is the notion of a smooth neighborhood deformation retract. A closed Frölicher subspace \(A\subseteq X\) has this property if there is a smooth neighborhood \(U\) of \(A\) and a smooth deformation of \(U\) into \(A\) that fixes \(A\) pointwise. Equivalently, the pair can be described by smooth control data: a function
\[
u\colon X\longrightarrow [0,1]
\]
whose zero set is \(A\), together with a flattened smooth homotopy
\[
K\colon X\times I\longrightarrow X
\]
such that \(K(x,0)=x\), \(K(a,t)=a\) for \(a\in A\), and \(K(x,1)\in A\) whenever \(x\) lies in the neighborhood selected by \(u\). These data are the smooth analogue of the Strøm or NDR structure familiar from ordinary topology.

Not every abstract smooth cofibration carries such neighborhood-control data. The relevant subclass consists of the closed, controlled cofibrations—often called NDR- or Strøm cofibrations—for which the homotopy extension property is accompanied by a smooth function detecting the subspace. For a closed Frölicher subspace \(A\subseteq X\), the following conditions are therefore equivalent:

1. \(A\) is a smooth neighborhood deformation retract of \(X\);
2. the inclusion \(A\hookrightarrow X\) is a closed controlled cofibration;
3. the inclusion admits smooth NDR data of the form described above.

One implication follows by using the neighborhood deformation to extend homotopies: points are first moved smoothly into the region where the prescribed homotopy is defined, and the flattened time parameter ensures that the resulting pieces fit together smoothly. Conversely, the control function and extension data associated with a controlled cofibration produce a neighborhood of \(A\) and a deformation of that neighborhood onto \(A\).

This equivalence supplies the technical foundation for cofiber constructions in the Frölicher category. Given a pointed controlled cofibration \(A\hookrightarrow X\), the quotient \(X/A\), or equivalently the associated smooth mapping cone, has the expected homotopy behavior. Iterating the cone and suspension constructions gives the right Puppe sequence
\[
A\longrightarrow X\longrightarrow X/A
   \longrightarrow \Sigma A\longrightarrow \Sigma X
   \longrightarrow \Sigma(X/A)\longrightarrow\cdots .
\]
Because the cofibration is controlled by smooth NDR data and the interval has been flattened at its endpoints, the connecting maps and the required homotopies are genuinely smooth. Thus smooth neighborhood deformation retracts provide precisely the well-behaved inclusions needed to reproduce the classical Puppe-sequence machinery within the homotopy theory of Frölicher spaces.

## Cofibrations and the Puppe Sequence

In algebraic topology, **cofibrations** provide a convenient framework for studying how one topological space is attached to another. A map \(i\colon A\to X\) is called a cofibration if it satisfies the homotopy extension property: every homotopy defined on \(A\) that agrees initially with a map on \(X\) can be extended over all of \(X\). The inclusion of a subcomplex \(A\subseteq X\) in a CW complex is a standard example.

Given a cofibration
\[
A \xrightarrow{i} X,
\]
one forms its **cofiber**
\[
X/A,
\]
obtained by collapsing \(A\) to a point. This produces a cofiber sequence
\[
A \xrightarrow{i} X \longrightarrow X/A.
\]

The construction can be continued using suspension. The resulting sequence is called the **Puppe sequence**, named after the mathematician Dieter Puppe:
\[
A \longrightarrow X \longrightarrow X/A
\longrightarrow \Sigma A \longrightarrow \Sigma X
\longrightarrow \Sigma(X/A) \longrightarrow \cdots .
\]
Here, \(\Sigma A\) denotes the reduced suspension of \(A\). The map \(X/A\to\Sigma A\) is the connecting map associated with the cofibration.

The Puppe sequence is important because applying a suitable homotopy-invariant functor turns it into a long exact sequence. For example, applying reduced homology gives
\[
\cdots \longrightarrow \widetilde H_n(A)
\longrightarrow \widetilde H_n(X)
\longrightarrow \widetilde H_n(X/A)
\longrightarrow \widetilde H_{n-1}(A)
\longrightarrow \cdots .
\]
Likewise, applying homotopy classes of pointed maps into or out of another space yields exact sequences that help calculate homotopy groups and analyze extensions of maps.

Thus, cofibrations and the Puppe sequence connect geometric attachment constructions with algebraic exactness. They are fundamental tools in homotopy theory, especially in the study of CW complexes, mapping cones, suspension, and generalized cohomology theories.

counterfactuals.output:
### Overview

In smooth homotopy theories, ordinary cofibrations can be too rigid because the piecewise formulas used in topological homotopy extension need not be smooth at their gluing parameters. A **weakened smooth cofibration** \(i\colon A\hookrightarrow X\) relaxes the smooth homotopy-extension property, typically by allowing a smooth reparametrization or a collar near the initial time. Thus, given a smooth map \(f\colon X\to Y\) and a homotopy \(H\colon A\times I\to Y\) with \(H(-,0)=f|_A\), one can extend \(H\) to \(X\times I\) after making it stationary near \(t=0\) or otherwise applying an admissible smoothing. This weakened property is still sufficient for the homotopy-theoretic constructions in which cofibrations are normally used.

The geometric models for such inclusions are smooth analogues of **neighborhood deformation retract (NDR) pairs**. One requires a smooth function measuring proximity to \(A\), together with a deformation of a neighborhood of \(A\) onto \(A\), fixed on \(A\). The neighborhood or “halo” supplies room for cutoff functions and smooth interpolation. Consequently, smooth NDR-type data imply the weakened homotopy-extension property; conversely, under suitable separation and regularity assumptions, weakened cofibrations can often be represented by such neighborhood deformation data. This identifies the abstract extension condition with a usable geometric criterion.

These cofibrations are especially important in constructing the **right Puppe sequence**. For a weakened smooth cofibration \(i\colon A\to X\), the smooth mapping cone
\[
C_i=X\cup_A CA
\]
is homotopically well behaved because the gluing along \(A\) supports the required extensions and smoothing. The resulting cofiber sequence
\[
A \xrightarrow{i} X \longrightarrow C_i
   \longrightarrow \Sigma A
   \xrightarrow{\Sigma i} \Sigma X
   \longrightarrow \Sigma C_i \longrightarrow \cdots
\]
is the right Puppe sequence in the smooth homotopy category. The weakened cofibration hypothesis ensures that mapping cones and quotients model homotopy cofibers, that successive connecting maps are well defined up to smooth homotopy, and that applying pointed homotopy classes into a target yields the expected exact sequence. Hence, the weakening preserves the essential formal role of cofibrations while accommodating the analytic constraints of smooth gluing.
